messages.subject: pvals.fnc and F statistic
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I wonder if anyone can help me with a question about pvals.fnc and lmer.

I'm running some re-analyses on a dataset analysed some years ago (2007), working with the languageR package.

In the earlier analyses, to obtain values for reporting, we used the then current version of pvals.fnc, with the following code:

x=pvals.fnc(model.lmer)
x$summary
x$anova

x$summary gave outputs like:

#                  Estimate Std.Error  DF t.value   pvals ci950 ci990 ci999
#(Intercept)        42.4514    2.1493 973  19.751 0.00000  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE
#typePsPr          -21.2240    1.7903 973 -11.855 0.00000  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE
#stressPN           -5.0640    0.8967 973  -5.648 0.00000  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE
#MorDMis             2.5627    1.7903 973   1.431 0.15275 FALSE FALSE FALSE
#typePsPr:stressPN   5.8140    1.0298 973   5.646 0.00000  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE
#stressPN:MorDMis    1.6569    1.0296 973   1.609 0.10794 FALSE FALSE FALSE

while x$anova gave e.g.

#            Df  SumSq MeanSq Denom         F   pvals
#type         1 7379.4 7379.4   973 113.83044 0.00000
#stress       1  398.6  398.6   973   6.14858 0.01332
#MorD         1  256.3  256.3   973   3.95354 0.04705
#type:stress  1 2069.7 2069.7   973  31.92602 0.00000
#stress:MorD  1  167.9  167.9   973   2.58993 0.10787

These days, based on a more recent version of languageR, my usual practice when running lmer is to do:

pvals.fnc(model.lmer)$fixed

This gives an output broadly similar to that of x$summary above, but with two sets of p values, one based on Monte Carlo Markov chains.

What I can't seem to obtain is an output like that of x$anova above, i.e. one that includes SumSq, MeanSq, df and F.

Does anyone know if this is possible?

If not, what can I report as the equivalent of (in ANOVA) the df, F and p for a main effect or interaction term?

Any advice very gratefully received.

Best wishes,

Rachel

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I'm trying to set up a model with a three-way contrast: between linguistic,
non-linguistic, and control. I'd like to compare all three to each other,
but for the moment, I'll focus on one set of Helmert contrasts:

  [,1] [,2]
l   -1   -1
n    1   -1
c    0    2

This should compare 1) linguistic to non-linguistic, and 2) 2 times control
to the average of linguistic and non-linguistic. So far so good.

My "baseline" model includes some control predictors, and more importantly,
random intercepts and slopes for subject and item. The slopes are by
"condition," and in this case I've used the contrasts, as follows:

baseline<-lmer(logRT~(1+contr1+contr2|subject)+(1+contr1+contr2|item)+controlpredictors)

This, in order to specify the "maximal" structure allowed/justified by the
data. So far still so good (right?).

Then I add the fixed effect contrasts:

ofInterest<-update(baseline,.~.+contr1+contr2)

The fixed effect output of this type of model indicates that, for one set
of RT's, the t-value for both contrasts "should be" significant. The output
for an identical model for a different set of RT's indicates that one (but
not the other) "should be" significant.

To get a usable significance, I have to use log-likelihood tests, because
pvals.fnc() won't work with random slopes (or is it just covariances?
Regardless...). But because my model comparison includes both contr1 and
contr2, the test isn't going to spit out individual significance values for
each, t-values or not. Is there some way to tell when contr1 is
significant, independent of the significance of contr2, in a model like the
one I've described? Can I rely on those t-values at all?

I'm happy to provide more information if it would clarify anything I've
muddied.

Jason

Hi Roger  (and still everyone),

After an educational link from an anonymous well-wisher, and a glance back
through Baayen (2008), I see that I'm confused. For the sake of anyone
reading this who still shares my earlier confusion, let me run through what
I've learned:

Those t-values are actually more reliable than I thought. My original
confusion came from reading a segment of Baayen too quickly - he recommends
pvals.fnc() for small datasets, only /after/ saying that t values are fine
for large datasets. "Large" here meaning something like thousands of
observations (though cf. your "hundreds," following Pinheiro & Bates, in
the link below).

The link I mentioned (
https://mailman.ucsd.edu/pipermail/ling-r-lang-l/2011-January/thread.html#198 -
Alex Fine's thread at the bottom) has basically the same answer from you
and Huge Quene. You cite Pinheiro and Bates (2000), and Quene cites Hox
(2010), who cites Raudenbush & Bryk (1992). Everyone gives slightly
different answers as to the recommended degrees of freedom, so anyone
interested should see the thread (and, I suppose, ideally the references),
but t values seem to work just fine in a pinch.

There are a couple of other interesting alternatives in that thread, which
I'd love to hear more about if they've developed more thoroughly, but for
now it sounds like I have my solution.

Thanks for clearing me up,
Jason

messages.body_plain:
I would recommend a slightly different approach.

(1) Start with a full RE model but without correlation parameters.
(2) Test for which REs you have reliable evidence for between-subject (betweein-item) variance components (drop-1 tests)
(3) Remove the non-significant variance components
(4) Estimate the correlation parameters only for the remaining model. (It does not make much sense to me to estimate a correlation parameter if you have evidence for reliable variance for one of the contributing components.)
(5)  Test whether (4) is significantly better than (4). It is actually not trivial to estimate reliable correlation parameters in our usual psycholinguistic or psychological expertiments.

Reinhold Kliegl

messages.body_plain:
It is highly unlikely that you have enough data to estimate so many variance components and correlation parameters. The program pretty much tells you as much. Further, taking a look at your variable names, I suspect that you did not distinguish between within-subject and between-subject  effects and also not between within-item and between-item effects. For example, a variable like cPresOrder is rarely a within-subject effect;  cLength is rarely a within-item effect. Random effects associated with subjects can only come from within-subject effects; random effects associated with items can only come from within-item effects. 

A quick stab at your two questions; I suspect they will be more cryptic than I want them to be.
(1) To get estimates of variance components without correlation parameters you need to specify them as independent components. The syntax in lmer to achieve this goes like this:

m1 <- lmer( y ~  a*b*c + (1 | id) + (0+a | id) + (0 + b | id) + (0 + c | id)  + (0 + a | item) + (0 + b | item) + (0 + c | item) ), data = xxx).

Note this assumes for now that a, b, c are within-subject and within-item factors and that they have two levels each (or represent contrasts derived from a complex design; using, e.g., contr.sum() as contrast attribute so that the intercept represents the grand mean). I also left out all the variance components associated with interactions between a, b, and c. 

(2)  Suppose you want to test whether you have evidence for a significant variance component associated with the within-subject effect of a. Then, you could specify m2 without this term

m2 <- lmer( y ~  a*b*c + (1 | id)  + (0 + b | id) + (0 + c | id)  + (0 + a | item) + (0 + b | item) + (0 + c | item) ), data = xxx).
anova(m1, m2)

yields a test whether dropping a  for id leads to a significant decrease in goodness of fit. If it does, you have evidence for reliable differences between subjects in the effect a. 

Obviously, there are quite a large number of decisions you have to make for such an analysis. I described how I am approaching such issues--currently. As far as I know, there is no generally accepted procedure, but I do think that it does not make much sense to estimate correlation parameters in the absence of reliable variance components related to them.  I am interested in comments on this position.

I am afraid LMMs are not as routine as F1/F2 ANOVAs. Therefore, actually, now I recommend that you get some local consultation on this analysis or find a script from an analysis of a different experiment that you can adopt for your analysis.  Good luck with your research.

Best
Reinhold Kliegl

Dear r-lang users,

I have a set of binary data from a 2 by 3 design study. I centered the
two-level predictor ('LHcenter': local & LD) but did not centered the
3 level predictor ('cond': A, B, & C). As you can see below in the
triangular matrix towards the end of the lmer output, there is
significant collinearity; the absolute values of some of the
correlations are above 0.6.

---8<----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
>glmer(true ~ cond * LHcenter + (1 | subject) + (1 | items), data=offlineTarget, family=binomial)

Generalized linear mixed model fit by the Laplace approximation
Formula: true ~ cond * LHcenter + (1 | subject) + (1 | items)
   Data: offlineTarget
   AIC   BIC   logLik deviance
  747.8 785.9 -365.9    731.8

Random effects:
 Groups        Name    Variance     Std.Dev.
 items     (Intercept)     0.13838     0.37199
 subject   (Intercept)    1.44652     1.20271
Number of obs: 864, groups: items, 30; subject, 29

Fixed effects:
                          Estimate    Std. Error     z value      Pr(>|z|)
(Intercept)           -0.09775      0.30932      -0.316      0.75199
condB                  0.62445      0.25534       2.446      0.01446   *
condC                  0.70552      0.27286       2.586      0.00972   **

condB:LHcenter   -2.31392      0.51162      -4.523      6.1e-06    ***
condC:LHcenter   -1.00381      0.54643      -1.837       0.06621   .
---
Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

Correlation of Fixed Effects:
                       (Intr)    condB    condC    LHcntr    cnB:LH
condB            -0.526
condC            -0.491    0.607
LHcenter        -0.085    0.130      0.118
cndB:LHcntr    0.070   -0.053     -0.093      -0.801
cndC:LHcntr    0.066   -0.093      0.033      -0.735     0.607
---8<----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

I also tested whether the interaction is significant by comparing the
full model with one without the interaction term:

glmer(true ~ cond * LHcenter + (1 | subject) + (1 | items),
data=offlineTarget, family=binomial)
glmer(true ~ cond  +  LHcenter + (1 | subject) + (1 | items),
data=offlineTarget, family=binomial)

And I observed a significant difference, suggesting that there is
significant interaction.

So I proceeded to conduct planned comparisons. To do so, I created a
new predictor in the table object by merging the two factors (a 3
level factor and a 2 level factor) together, resulting in a new factor
named 'posthoc_cond' with 6 levels: Local_A, Local_B, Local_C, LD_A,
LD_B, & LD_C

I conducted glmer WITHOUT centering the 6-level fixed predictor 'posthoc_cond'.

posthoc_result = glmer(true~posthoc_cond + (1|subject) + (1|item),
data=offlineTarget, family="binomial")

and then use glht() from 'multcomp' to conduct paired comparisons.

The problem with posthoc_result, again, is high collinearity (see below)
---8<----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Correlation of Fixed Effects:

psthc_cndA_    -0.865
psthc_cB_LD    -0.835  0.712
psthc_cndB_    -0.944  0.896         0.734
psthc_cC_LD    -0.928  0.810        0.779      0.896
psthc_cndC_     -0.891  0.925        0.710      0.914      0.834
---8<----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

So my question is, in my case, what can be done to reduce
collinearity. It seems that centering those multi-level predictors is
not applicable in my case since I am interested in whether different
levels of the fixed predictors have different means. Centering these
multilevel predictors would not allow me to test that.

Thank you in advance for your help!!


Best,
Xiao

> spurious significance or it may hide significance. So I want to make
> sure that the results I obtained are not due to collinearity.

Hi Xiao,

By "hide significance" I think you mean increase rate of Type II errors, or false negatives -- that is, reduce the chance that 
you will find a significant effect of a predictor that truly does have an effect on your dependent variable.  Is this what you mean?  If so, yes, collinearity can do this.

As for causing spurious significance, by which I think you mean increasing the rate of Type I error above nominal (or whatever rate it would be without multicollinearity) -- this should not happen.  If you have seen such an example given concretely, perhaps you could repost the example for the list and we can discuss it?

Best

Roger

Hi,

I think part of my concern is Type 1 and Type 2 Errors. From my
experience with my own data, Type II error is a big concern, as I've
encountered cases where reducing collinearity changes test results
from non-significant to highly significant.

A tutorial that Dr. Jaeger created on mixed effects model does mention
that Type 1 error does not increase much in the presence of
collinearity. But if I recall correctly, there is an example in the
tutorial using the lexdec dataset where the presence of extremely high
collinearity causes an (?)overestimate of significance.

So in essence, without being able to reduce collinearity, I am afraid
of not being able to detect significances when there are in fact
significant differences (or vice versa), and interpreting coefficient
estimates is also problematic.

Thanks.

Best,
Xiao
